name: Forward Deployed Engineering
description: Work with customers inside their environment, turn messy problems into working software, and carry what you learn back to the product.

topics.name: Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE)
topics.summary: Scope real customer problems, prototype against real data, evaluate before trusting, ship inside the customer's controls, measure impact, and hand off so the work outlives you.

lessons.title: What a forward deployed engineer does
lessons.content:
A forward deployed engineer (FDE) is a software engineer who works inside a customer's environment to build, deploy, and operate technical solutions. The role sits between product engineering, solutions engineering, implementation, and customer success, and it is still defined differently from company to company. Some teams call it forward deployed software engineer (FDSE) or customer-embedded engineer.

## Where the role came from

The model is usually traced to Palantir, which used embedded engineers early on to get its software working inside large organizations. Newer AI companies have adopted a variant often called the forward deployed AI engineer, focused on deploying language models and agents. The core idea is the same in both: the engineer goes to where the problem lives instead of asking the customer to bring the problem to the product.

## What the job is, in practice

Working directly with customers is the top duty in most job descriptions, and the role is an engineering position rather than a sales one. A FDE typically does four kinds of work:

- **Discovery**: learn how the work really gets done, including the workarounds nobody documents
- **Build**: connect systems, write code, and configure the product for one environment
- **Deploy and operate**: go through the customer's security review, change process, and network rules, then keep the solution running
- **Feed the product**: turn repeated customizations into evidence and requests the product team can act on

## The stakeholders you are balancing

- **The customer's operators**, who live with the workflow every day and will judge the result
- **The customer's sponsor**, who needs a measurable outcome and a reason to keep funding it
- **Your product team**, who owns the platform and will inherit whatever you build
- **Implementation and customer success**, who take over once the work is repeatable

## Qualities that separate strong FDEs

- **Software fundamentals**: you can read unfamiliar code, debug integrations, and write production-quality changes
- **Judgment under ambiguity**: the problem definition is usually incomplete, and you have to decide what to build
- **Plain communication**: you explain trade-offs to people who will never read the code
- **Scope discipline**: you say no, or "not in this phase", without losing the customer

## Common traps

- Building a one-off for one customer that the product cannot support later
- Becoming the permanent operator of something that should have been handed off
- Treating the first demo as the finish line
- Taking every request from the most vocal customer and losing the thread of the success measure

## Further reading

- [Bloomberry: analysis of forward deployed engineer job postings](https://bloomberry.com/blog/?p=2502)
- [FullStack: the seven skills that define a forward-deployed engineer](https://www.fullstack.com/blog/the-seven-skills-that-define-a-forward-deployed-engineer)
- [Umbrex: the forward deployed engineer playbook](https://umbrex.com/resources/the-forward-deployed-engineer-playbook/delivery-playbooks-by-engagement-type/)

lessons.title: Discovery: finding the problem worth solving
lessons.content:
The first version of a customer problem is rarely the real one. Discovery is the work of finding the problem worth solving, proving you can access what it needs, and agreeing on how success will be measured. Most failed deployments trace back to a weak discovery, not a weak build.

## Start with the workflow, not the wish

Ask the people who do the work to walk you through the last time they did it, step by step. Capture the inputs, the handoffs, the approvals, the spreadsheets nobody mentions, and the places where things go wrong. Draw the workflow map yourself. Customers correct a drawing faster than they describe a process.

Useful questions:

- What triggers this work, and how often does it happen?
- What do you do when the input is missing, late, or wrong?
- Who do you ask when you are stuck, and how long does that take?
- What would make you stop using the new process within a month?

## Interview the people with the constraints

The person who asked for the project is often not the person who will live with it. Speak to the operator who does the daily work, the approver who signs off, the person who handles exceptions, and the owner of the data. Their constraints usually decide the difference between a demo and a deployment.

## Write a value hypothesis

Before building, state the change you expect in one sentence: "If we automate matching of shipment exceptions, the team clears backlog in two days instead of six, saving about 40 hours a week." A value hypothesis forces you to name the metric, the baseline, the expected change, and the owner of the result. It also tells you quickly if the project is not worth doing.

Record the current value of the metric before any change. A baseline taken during an unusually quiet or busy period will mislead you later.

## Separate must-haves from later

- **Must-have**: the workflow cannot run without it
- **Should-have**: it saves real time but has a workaround
- **Later**: interesting, but not tied to the success measure

Write the scope down and confirm it in writing. Every later change request should be classified as a product gap, a reusable pattern, a customer-specific extension, services work, or out of scope. That classification keeps one enthusiastic customer from consuming the whole team.

## Check feasibility before the timeline

Confirm three things before you commit to a date:

- **Access**: you can reach the data and systems, in a sandbox if the customer requires it
- **Time**: the operators and the sponsor will give the time the project needs
- **Destination**: someone is ready to act on the output

A project that fails on access in week one is a cheap failure. The same failure in week six is expensive.

## Know when not to start

Do not start a proof of value without a named sponsor, agreed access, and a success measure written down. Without those, a successful prototype will still not get used.

## Further reading

- [Perspective AI: how forward deployed engineers run customer discovery](https://getperspective.ai/blog/how-forward-deployed-engineers-run-customer-discovery-2026)
- [FDE Academy: project lifecycle from discovery to deployment](https://fde.academy/blog/fde-project-lifecycle-from-discovery-to-deployment)

lessons.title: Prototype against real data, then decide
lessons.content:
A prototype answers one question: does this approach work on this customer's real data? It is meant to be looked at, tested, and often thrown away. Treating it as production code too early wastes time and hides the decisions you still need to make.

## Use real data as early as the policies allow

Synthetic data hides what matters: missing fields, inconsistent formats, duplicate records, and edge cases nobody documented. Get a representative sample as early as the customer's rules permit, and keep it inside the customer's environment if the agreement requires it.

## Build the thinnest end-to-end path

Connect input to output before you perfect any one step. A rough pipeline that handles most common cases end to end teaches more than a perfect parser that never reaches a user. Once the path works, improve the step that fails most often.

## Show a working version every few days

A working screen or a real sample output gets better feedback than a slide. Demo the rough version, record what the operator said, and note which requests they actually needed versus which they asked for in the abstract.

## Build an evaluation harness early

Before the prototype grows, write down the cases it must get right. Collect real examples with known correct outcomes, including the hard ones, and run the prototype against them every time it changes. The harness is what lets you change things without guessing whether you broke something. The evaluation and guardrails lesson covers this in depth.

## Mark what is disposable

Label prototype code clearly. Keep the parts that encode knowledge about the problem, such as matching rules, exception categories, and the definition of a good outcome. Rewrite the parts that were only scaffolding.

## Decide when to harden

Move toward production when all of these hold:

- The success measure and its baseline are agreed
- The common cases work on real data
- The failure modes you still need to handle are named
- Someone other than you could run it from your documentation

If one of these is missing, keep iterating. A prototype that works for one person is not a deployment.

## What hardening adds

- **Tests** for the business rules, using real examples from discovery as fixtures
- **Configuration** for anything that differs between customers, instead of code branches
- **Structured logs** that record decisions and failures without storing sensitive fields
- **Safe failure** that routes uncertain cases to a person instead of guessing
- **A rollback path** that returns the customer to the old process within minutes

Do not skip the rollback path. It is often the reason a customer agrees to try the next change.

## Further reading

- [Scaler: the forward deployed engineer playbook](https://www.scaler.com/topics/the-forward-deployed-engineer-playbook/)
- [Rocketlane: the FDE blueprint for professional services leaders](https://www.rocketlane.com/blogs/fde-blueprint)

lessons.title: Working safely inside customer systems
lessons.content:
FDEs often touch data they do not own, in systems they did not design, under rules they must follow exactly. Most production work runs through the customer's security review, network policy, and change process. Planning for those early is what makes a deployment possible at all.

## Start with the smallest access that works

Request read-only access to a sandbox or a copy of the data first. Ask for write access only when a specific step needs it, and only for the systems and tables that step touches. Record each grant with its purpose and the person who approved it.

## Know what counts as sensitive

- Find out which fields are personal, financial, health-related, or otherwise regulated before you load anything
- Remove or mask fields the task does not need
- Keep data in the customer's environment when their agreement requires it
- Never paste real records into tickets, chat threads, or public examples

If a sample must leave the environment, redact it first and check the redaction a second time.

## Write down integration contracts

For every integration, document the inputs and outputs: field names, types, units, time zones, and what "empty" means. Many integration failures are disagreements about these details. They are easy to test once they are written down.

## Secure the path, not only the endpoint

- Store credentials in the customer's secret manager, never in code or config files in the repository
- Give each automated process the least privilege that lets it do its job
- Log who or what triggered each action and what it changed
- Re-check the automation's permissions whenever its scope grows

## Prepare for the security review

Expect the customer's security team to review the design before go-live. Bring a short document with the data flows, what is stored and for how long, the access list, the failure modes, and who can turn the system off. A clear document shortens the review. A missing one stalls the project for weeks.

## Plan the network and change path early

Ask early how changes reach production in the customer's environment: which approvals they need, which windows they allow, and how rollbacks are handled. A solution that is ready on Friday but cannot pass change control until next quarter is not ready.

## Further reading

- [Leanware: forward deployed engineer role, responsibilities, and use cases](https://leanware.co/insights/forward-deployed-engineer-role-use-cases)

lessons.title: Evaluate AI solutions before customers rely on them
lessons.content:
When a solution uses a language model or another probabilistic component, you need evidence that it is good enough for the task, and a plan for when it is not. Evaluation is what turns a promising demo into something a customer can depend on. One skills framework for FDE work groups evals and guardrails as core skills alongside software engineering, which reflects how much AI deployments depend on them.

## Build the evaluation set

Collect 30 to 100 real examples with the correct outcome or decision. Include three groups:

- **Common cases**, in the proportions they really occur
- **Hard cases**, such as ambiguous inputs and conflicting records
- **Negative cases**, where the correct answer is "not enough information" or "send to a person"

Agree the set with the operators who know the right answers. Freeze the version you agreed on, and add new cases as production surfaces them. Keep it under version control so changes are visible.

## Measure what the workflow cares about

A single overall accuracy score hides the failures that cost the most. Track these separately:

- **Decision accuracy** on the decisions the customer cares about
- **Escalation rate**, the share of cases routed to a person
- **Cost of a wrong answer**, in the customer's terms, such as a wrong payment or a missed shipment
- **Stability**, meaning whether the same input gives the same output across runs

A system that is 90 percent accurate but silently wrong on the expensive 10 percent is worse than one that is 85 percent accurate and flags its uncertain cases.

## Design for uncertainty

- **Validate outputs** against a schema before they reach another system
- **Set confidence thresholds** on the evaluation set, not by feel
- **Route uncertain cases** to a reviewer with the evidence they need
- **Record the reviewer's decision** and feed it back into the evaluation set

## Guard against regressions

Re-run the evaluation set whenever the prompt, the model version, the retrieval source, or the validation rules change. Compare with the last accepted result and block the change if a key measure drops, even when the overall number rises.

## Log for reproduction

Record the input, the version of every component involved, the output, and the reason for any routing decision. Mask sensitive fields before logging. When a customer reports a wrong result, you need to reproduce it in minutes, not days.

## Further reading

- [Beetroot: forward deployed engineering, the role between AI pilots and production](https://beetroot.co/ai-ml/forward-deployed-engineering-the-role-between-ai-pilots-and-production/)
- [Perspective AI: forward deployed engineer tech stack in 2026](https://getperspective.ai/blog/fde-tech-stack-2026-tools-forward-deployed-engineers-actually-ship)

lessons.title: From deployment to ownership
lessons.content:
Going live is the start of operating the solution. Many engagements fail at handoff, not at launch: the FDE stays attached, ownership stays unclear, and the customer cannot run what was built. Plan the handoff from the first week.

## Split the work clearly

A common pattern separates two roles:

- **The implementation lead** owns the project plan, milestones, dependencies, training, and go-live coordination
- **The FDE** owns field technical problem-solving, workflow fit, prototype validation, and the blockers only an engineer can clear

This split stops the FDE from becoming the project manager by default. It also means the project does not stall when the FDE is in a technical debugging session.

## Define exit criteria before go-live

Decide what "handed off" means in writing. A reasonable set:

- The first workflow is live, or ready to go live, on real data
- The customer owner has accepted ownership, by name
- Support paths are documented, including response times and escalation
- The runbook, evaluation set, and list of known limitations are in the customer's hands
- The customer's operators have run the exception path without you

When these are met, the FDE hands back to implementation or customer success.

## Document the repeatable pattern

Once a deployment pattern works, write it down before moving on. Note the integration steps, the configuration choices, the common failure modes, and the questions that predicted success. Then move the repeatable parts to implementation or the customer's technical team. Staying attached after the work is repeatable creates dependence on one engineer.

## Monitor outcomes, not only uptime

Alongside technical health checks, track the measures from discovery: match rate, escalation share, time per case. Set alerts when they drift from the baseline. A service can be healthy and still failing its job.

## Run a structured handover

- Walk the customer's operators through the review queue and the exception paths
- Hand over integration notes, including each customer system's quirks
- Confirm in writing who owns each component
- Rehearse one failure scenario together and agree the response

## Feed the product

After go-live, review every customization. Each should end in one of three places: removed, kept as explicit configuration with an owner, or turned into a product request with evidence. Repeated requests from several customers are the strongest signal the product team will get.

## Watch for rescue becoming routine

If the FDE team keeps rescuing troubled deployments, the cause is usually upstream: the product, the sales process, the implementation plan, or support. A rescue should lead to a root-cause fix, not to a habit.

## Further reading

- [Umbrex: delivery playbooks by engagement type](https://umbrex.com/resources/the-forward-deployed-engineer-playbook/delivery-playbooks-by-engagement-type/)

lessons.title: Measuring impact and return on investment
lessons.content:
An FDE project succeeds when the customer's measure moves and stays moved. Plan the measurement before the build, so the result is evidence rather than opinion.

## Set the baseline first

Record the current value of each success measure over a representative period. Note seasonality, staffing changes, and anything else that could move the number without your help. A baseline from an unusually quiet month will overstate your results.

## Choose a fair comparison

- **Before and after**: simple, but exposed to other changes happening at the same time
- **Parallel run**: the old and new process handle the same work, and the outcomes are compared
- **Staged rollout**: some teams switch first, and the rest act as a comparison group

Use the simplest design the customer will accept, and state its limits in the report.

## Build a value case

A basic return calculation uses four inputs:

- **Benefit**: the measured change, valued in money or in risk avoided
- **One-time cost**: engineering time, integration work, and the customer's own staff time
- **Ongoing cost**: infrastructure, licenses, monitoring, and model or data maintenance
- **Payback period**: one-time cost divided by monthly net benefit

Be conservative. Count only the change you can trace to the solution, and show a range instead of a single figure.

## Track the outcome in the customer's terms

The customer cares about the number they already report: cases closed, invoices corrected, days to first transaction. Use those measures rather than internal ones such as model accuracy alone. Model metrics support the story; the business metric tells it.

## Report what did not work

A report that lists only successes will not be trusted. Include the cases the solution handled badly, how often human review was needed, and what the team changed in response. Customers who see the limits clearly are more likely to expand the project.

## Decide what happens next

End each measurement cycle with a recommendation: expand, change the scope, or stop. Tie it to the numbers and name the person who makes the call. A measurement that does not change a decision was not worth the effort.

## Further reading

- [FDE Academy: forward deployed engineer playbook](https://fde.academy/blog/forward-deployed-engineer-playbook)

lessons.title: Communicating trade-offs and risks
lessons.content:
FDEs make decisions in front of customers, often with incomplete information and tight deadlines. Clear communication keeps those decisions trusted and makes risks visible while they are still cheap to fix.

## Present options, not only an answer

For each decision, compare two or three options on the same terms: time to value, ongoing effort, main risk, and whether the choice can be reversed. Recommend one and say why. Let the customer choose with the full picture.

| Option | Time to value | Ongoing effort | Main risk | Reversible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Configure the existing product | 2 weeks | Low | Missing edge cases | Yes |
| Build a custom connector | 6 weeks | Medium | Maintenance burden | Partly |
| Keep the manual process for now | None | High | Continued errors | Yes |

## Keep updates short and regular

A weekly update with progress, decisions made, open risks, and what you need from the customer is more useful than a long report. Keep it specific. Name an owner and a due date for every open item.

## Escalate early, with a proposal

If a deadline, a data quality issue, or a scope change threatens the success measure, raise it the same week. Bring a proposed fix with the problem. People forgive a problem they heard about early; they rarely forgive one they found at the review.

## Classify every new request

When a request arrives mid-project, classify it before you answer: product gap, reusable pattern, customer-specific extension, services work, or out of scope. Then say where it goes. This keeps the success measure in view and makes trade-offs visible to the sponsor.

## Say what you do not know

State each assumption and how confident you are in it. "We tested this on 200 records and expect the same pattern on the rest" tells the customer what to plan around. A stated uncertainty is far easier to manage than a surprise.

## Disagree in private, commit in public

Raise disagreements in a working session before the meeting where the decision is announced. Once the decision is made, deliver it well, and record your concern so the outcome can be reviewed later.

## Further reading

- [FullStack: the seven skills that define a forward-deployed engineer](https://www.fullstack.com/blog/the-seven-skills-that-define-a-forward-deployed-engineer)
